Preface to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The preface states: The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is the wisdom that embodies the most refined and unimpeded principle. Its ultimate realization consists of three aspects.

It is said that there are three aspects: the true mark (*dharmatā*), contemplative illumination (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), and words (*vyañjana*). These three differ in appearance but are identical in essence; they are all *prajñā*.
They do not arise from one another, nor do they contain one another; yet they cannot be separated, nor can they be conjoined. If one were to divide what is not divided, the Sūtra says:
"The realm of inconceivable wisdom is the true mark; the light of inconceivable wisdom is contemplation."
The illumination is the inconceivable torch of wisdom; the characters are the true reality (*dharmatā*), which is the essence of the sutra.

Contemplative observation is the central tenet of the sutra, while the characters are its function. The tenet serves to guide all virtues toward the convergence of the signless (*animitta*) and the ultimate;
the function serves to sweep away all delusions, opening the spirit for awakening to its full extent.
The ultimate reality is thus; its essence is not so. Abiding naturally in the Middle Way, it is secure and unmoving, silently containing all wonders and pervading boundlessly in all directions.
Therefore, it is able to serve as the source from which the myriad things originate. The Sage unifies the One to cultivate the Three, and through the Three, attains the One.
To achieve this is called *pāramitā*; to abide in this is called the Secret Treasury. It is vast and great indeed!

This can be contemplated; yet it is truly lamentable that sentient beings, being born again and again, cling to existence and grasp at emptiness, remaining confined within the cage of conditioned phenomena and unable to know how to escape on their own.

Postscript to the *Zhi Guan* (Cessation and Contemplation) by the Chan Master of Nanyue:
The application of cessation and contemplation is rooted in clarity and stillness; clarity and stillness are virtues rooted in the single nature (*ekadhātu*).

The essence of this nature is inherently awakened, which is called "luminous awakening" (*prabhāsvara-bodhi*); its essence is inherently quiescent, which is called "stillness. This non-duality of luminosity and stillness is termed the "substance" (*tattva*), and this substance has no location.
When divided, clarity, stillness, and tranquility find their locus; when nothing is lacking, clarity and stillness are present. To speak of their substance (*tǐ*), it is not one yet ever one;
to speak of their qualities (*dé*), they are not two yet ever two. It is merely divided yet not divided, merely one yet not one.
Substance and qualities do not change, yet we forcibly name them the "nature" (*prakṛti*) of all phenomena; substance and qualities have no abiding place, yet we forcibly name them...
The source of the myriad dharmas—what, then, are these "myriad dharmas"? It is said that they are produced by the totality of luminous stillness. Why is this so?
It is because the luminosity of primordial enlightenment (*anādikāla-ādi-bodhi*), through its forceful illumination, gives rise to cognition and thereby deludes itself; this is called "obscurity.

Because the beginningless, non-abiding source follows conditions and arises in dependence upon them, it becomes disordered of its own accord; this is called "movement. Thus, there is obscurity and movement.
Once the myriad dharmas have been produced, they are like flowers in the sky seen by one who presses upon their eyes; how could they be anything other than that [mind]? Therefore it is said:
"Unchanging yet following conditions, it is called mind; following conditions yet unchanging, it is called nature. Mind is dark and active; nature is luminous and still.
If one knows that from time immemorial the luminous has become dark, then one can realize that the active is now still. Thus it is.
The Sage perceives that its darkness and movement can be immediately engaged with, while its clarity and stillness can be returned to.

Therefore, he uses stillness to instruct on cessation, thereby ceasing its movement; he uses clarity to teach observation, thereby observing its darkness. He causes [the practitioner] to investigate a single thought, such that movement is immediately stillness and darkness is immediately clarity.
Once darkness and movement have ceased, the myriad dharmas naturally vanish; there remains only clarity and stillness.
This essence is the Perfect and Sudden; it is the Unconditioned; it is the practice of the Tathāgata.

When illumination brings nature to fulfillment through cultivation, and cultivation is perfected so that function ceases, who can discuss "stopping" (śamatha) and "contemplation" (vipaśyanā)? When the essence is manifest and nature is dissolved, there is neither clarity nor stillness;

To clarify that all natures are neither conjoined nor dispersed, but are simply so of themselves—this is called the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena;

it is intended to make it easy for people to comprehend. Thereafter, one demonstrates that in a single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*), the three thousand realms are all empty; in a single thought-moment, the three thousand realms are all provisional;

and within a single thought-moment, the three thousand realms are all the Middle Way. Thus, one perfects the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) and contemplates the three truths (*tisraḥ satyāni*) in their perfection, thereby clarifying all modes of cultivation.
It is great wisdom and great practice; it is swift without being stirred, called the Great White Ox Cart, which causes people to enter suddenly.

Thus, from cause to fruit, one attains it without shifting for a single thought. Sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one realizes perfect awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), subdues Māra, preaches the Dharma, and delivers sentient beings.
Upon entering *nirvāṇa*, one’s duties are completed. Using the verse of Nāgārjuna: "Dependent origination is itself emptiness."
What are the ten dharma-realms that are identical through the provisional being the middle? The "ten" comprehensively encompasses all phenomena, and the "three truths" constitute the realms.
Why is this so? It is because Buddhas take the Middle Way as their dharma-realm; Bodhisattvas take the conventional as their dharma-realm;
and Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas alike take emptiness as their dharma-realm. [The same applies to] those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals...
Humans and devas alike take the dharma of arising through causes and conditions as the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Although emptiness, the provisional, and the middle are three, they are one;
although the ten realms are ten, they are also one. Thus, each realm mutually contains the others—one possessing all nine—just as imperial jewels reflect one another to form a hundred Dharma-realms.
One cause-and-condition is all cause-and-conditions; one emptiness is all [emptinesses].
"Emptiness is one, and all are provisional; within the one, all are real. It is precisely because of this that the 'Three Thousand' are so called.
What, then, does this mean? Regarding the principles for establishing the realms, there are ten, namely:
such appearance, such nature, such substance, such power, such function, such cause, such condition, such fruit, such retribution, and such inclusion."

"This is the ultimate equality of the beginning and the end"—this is the summary. These ten dharmas, when present in a Buddha, are the Middle Way, the Real, the Permanent, the Three Wisdoms, the Five Eyes, the Ten Powers, the Four Fearlessnesses, and the Unshared Dharmas;

when present in a Bodhisattva, they are the Provisional, the Expedient, the Flourishing, the Permanent, the Myriad Practices, and the Four Means of Integration; when present in the Two Vehicles, they are Emptiness and the Expedient.
To be the three liberations, the four aridities, the untainted, and nirvana;

to be inversion for ordinary beings, delusion, outflow, hindrance, entanglement, the accumulation of affliction, and birth-and-death—these are the distinctions. Taken collectively, those hundred realms constitute a thousand dharmas;
further distributed across the various hundred realms, they become the three thousand worlds, forming the three thousand dharmas. Thus, the hundred realms and the three thousand [are one].
First, this single thought-moment is neither before nor after, nor do its parts contain one another;

it is unified by a central principle and converged upon a fundamental source, which must ultimately return to the inconceivable treasury of the three truths, the three dharmas, and the three virtues. Alas!

Since the dharma of the single thought-moment is thus, when one extends this principle to all else, every instance of the Buddha-dharma and every instance of the sentient-being-dharma are likewise so.
Indeed, the Sūtra says: "As it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha; as it is with the Buddha, so it is with sentient beings.

Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. Is this not what is meant? Having understood this, one should observe that in daily life, whenever a single thought arises, it necessarily belongs to one realm.
One should then illuminate this realm to see whether it is ninefold or the Buddha-nature. If it is ninefold, it is said that it arises through partiality according to deluded emotion.
The Buddha regards ignorance as the perfect contemplation of principle and calls it Great Wisdom (*mahāprajñā*). The thoughts of the nine realms are not distinct from the mind of the Buddha-realm;

this is precisely what serves as the mirror for discerning right and wrong. What is wrong is illuminated so that it may become right, and what is right is protected so that it may be brought into practice.
As the Sūtra says: "The liberation of all Buddhas should be sought within the mental activities of sentient beings; by practicing upon what is considered a non-path, one is able to reach [the goal]."
This is what is meant by the Buddha-way. Thus, although the eyes are on the face, they must look into a mirror to correct the countenance;
the mind, though actually originating from within, must rely on external conditions to direct its deliberations. Since the numinous spirit is hidden and subtle, it is difficult to perceive;

and since mental phenomena are turbulent and racing, they are not easy to restrain. Therefore, we now draw the mind outward to depict the images of those who have ascended or sunk, while maintaining the will within.
Having observed the transformations between right and wrong, I then disciplined my mind to inwardly illuminate the True Path.

Based on this clarity, I titled this work "The Diagram of the Ten Dharma Realms for Contemplating the Mind in the Perfect and Sudden Teaching. From the single character "One Mind," I branch out into the ten realms;

furthermore, I employ black and white threads to interweave them like a string of pearls, demonstrating that each realm contains all nine others, thus forming the hundred dharma realms. This is practiced according to the sequence of the days.

For those who peruse this work on physiognomy and wish to penetrate deeply into the nature [of beings], I request they examine the prefaces in detail; for those who wish to become proficient in cultivation, they should observe the various diagrams and forms.
Buddha-realm.

If a person, by virtue of reading the *Pūrṇa-sūtra* and hearing the teachings of a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), gives rise to pure faith, they will believe that the nature of the three paths within their own single thought-moment is itself the nature of the three virtues:
the path of suffering is the *dharmakāya*, afflictions are *prajñā*, and karmic fetters are liberation. Thus, the *dharmakāya* is ultimate, *prajñā* is pure, and liberation is sovereign.
The ultimate perfection of all things is the ultimate perfection of prajñā-liberation;
the ultimate purity of the single pure Dharmakāya is also the purity of liberation. The single sovereignty of all sovereignties is the sovereignty of the Dharmakāya-prajñā.
Thus, it is three in one and one in three; neither vertical nor horizontal, neither identical nor different—the Dharmakāya is eternal.

Abiding in the remainder [of dharmas], they are likewise eternally abiding, blissful, self, and pure; this is the secret treasury of the four virtues of permanence, bliss, and so forth, which pervades all places.
Since all phenomena are entirely the Buddha-dharma, once one has gained faith in this, one binds the mind to the object and the object to the mind.
With the mind and object continuing in succession from moment to moment without interruption, one will certainly perceive the *dharmatā*. Even if they have not yet met...
One should rely upon the four truths—which are ultimately one, real, and unconditioned—to give rise to the four great vows. Within that which is nothing to be sought, I therefore seek it:

by relying on the aforementioned path of suffering, one gives rise to the first vow for those who have not yet crossed over; by [relying on] afflictions and karma, one gives rise to the second vow for those who have not yet been liberated;
and by [relying on] the path of suffering itself, which is the Dharma-body, one gives rise to [the third vow].
Regarding the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), one makes a single vow: to cause those who have not yet attained *nirvāṇa* to attain it.

Regarding the fact that afflictions are themselves bodhi, which is the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), one makes a single vow: to cause those who are not yet at peace to find peace. One should skillfully settle the mind so that the Four Great Vows are not lost.

By practicing these ten dharmas in this sequence, one will certainly enter the five grades (*pañca-varga*). Those in the stages of the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) and partial realization are called Buddhas.
The Dharma-realm and the Bodhisattva-realm:

if one contemplates that the faculties and objects within a single thought-moment are the root of both delusion and awakening, then because of delusion there are the ten realms of suffering and its accumulation, and because of awakening... [there is the cessation and the path].
Then, there are the four noble paths that extinguish [afflictions]; based on these immeasurable Four Noble Truths, one gives rise to immeasurable vows:

to cause those who have not crossed over to cross over, those who are not liberated to be liberated, those who are not at peace to find peace, and those who have not attained nirvāṇa to attain nirvāṇa.

With skillful means for delivering sentient beings and gazing upon all things with eyes of compassion, one shares the merit accumulated in this way with all sentient beings; thus, one gives rise to a single [thought of enlightenment].
Mindfulness is called the Bodhisattva-dharmadhātu.

When thoughts arise regarding the sense bases and objects of the Pratyekabuddha-dhātu, one realizes that they arise from ignorance; because they arise from ignorance, there is volitional formation (*saṃskāra*), and volitional formation invites name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

From birth through old age and death, the continuity across the three periods of time is like a whirling firebrand; its causes and conditions are fundamentally empty, a phantom manifestation lacking reality.

Seeking the bliss of spontaneous wisdom, one delights in solitary, virtuous, and tranquil contemplation, deeply immersing oneself in the emptiness of the mind and dwelling in meditative concentration. Although one attains the fruits of the Path, one does not seek to transform others.

Furthermore, there are those who contemplate the flourishing and falling of all things, awakening to the impermanence of the world and attaining the Path through the realization of emptiness; these are called [the practitioners of] Emptiness.
A solitary realizer who practices in this manner is called one whose dharma-realm is that of a pratyekabuddha.

As for the realm of the śrāvaka, because there is at least a single moment of dependence upon form and mind through the conditions of faculties and objects, there is suffering due to afflictions and accumulation due to [craving]. One feels weary of them.
Since suffering is to be abandoned and its origin is not the antidote, how can one cultivate the sixteen contemplations and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment based on the Four Noble Truths?

One must do so with the urgency of one whose hair is on fire. By means of the four roots of goodness, one enters the untainted state and realizes the two types of nirvana through the four fruits of the śramaṇa.
Those who encounter only partial truth fail to attain the Buddha-dharma; they do not long for transformation, being like a deer that bounds alone without looking back.
The collective state of such a single thought is called the dharma-realm of the śrāvakas.
As for the dharma-realm of the devas,
if their thoughts arise with great joy in celestial pleasures, they cultivate their virtuous minds and aspire for future retribution, maintaining the purity of their fasts and precepts.
Providing food for śramaṇas, constructing stūpas and temples, as well as images of the Buddha, transcribing Mahāyāna sūtras, and providing relief to the poor and the sick;

fully practicing both the abstention from and the performance of the ten wholesome dharmas so that one’s nature spontaneously becomes perfected; restraining the six sense faculties so that the six consciousnesses do not dissipate and the six sensory objects do not enter;
and attaining the dhyānas of the desire realm as well as the concentrations of the form and formless realms, whereby body and mind are tranquil—these three.
When one's karma is thus disciplined and excellent, a single thought-moment is called the celestial dharma-realm (*deva-dharmadhātu*). As for the human dharma-realm (*manuṣya-dharmadhātu*),
if one establishes virtue through the five constants in every thought-moment and cultivates the person through the five precepts, being loyal to the state and filial to the family—

Xiaokuan dwelt among the multitude with integrity, ever maintaining sincerity and deferring virtue to others while taking blame upon herself. She honored her superiors and showed compassion to those below;
she provided for the solitary and relieved the poor. Guilt and shame were held within her heart, and kindness and harmony were her nature.

She deeply believed in cause and effect and revered the Triple Gem, diligently practicing the precepts of fasting and establishing stupas and monasteries. She sought only worldly happiness, and her mind was never distracted by greed or attachment.
To be attached to one's kin and retinue is called the human realm (*manuṣya-dhātu*).
As for the asura realm, although they may,
in every thought-moment, cultivate goodness, practice giving, and observe the precepts, they are characterized by much suspicion, doubt, and hesitation.
The meritorious deeds they cultivate are mostly for the sake of surpassing others; seeing people practice goodness, their hearts are full of jealousy;

they are arrogant, conceited, and self-important, cherishing themselves while disparaging others; they desire others to submit to them and cannot tolerate humility or self-effacement. Like a soaring falcon looking down from on high, they outwardly display benevolence and righteousness while inwardly lacking true virtue;
when discussing matters before a crowd, they exaggerate their own importance and fail to follow correct principles, feeling no shame.
O worthy one, when the mind acts in such a way, that is the realm of asuras;
it is the realm of hungry ghosts if,
in every thought-moment, one is without shame or remorse, greedily seeking without satiety, stingy and miserly, not giving away even a single hair’s breadth.
They exploit others to amass wealth for themselves; when they see others practicing charity, they erect obstacles; when they see others gaining profit, their hearts burn with resentment.
They are by nature full of flattery and crookedness, constantly giving rise to false views. Before others they maintain a proper countenance, but in private they act with license.
They break their fasts and violate the precepts, indulging greedily in food and drink. They do not believe in sin or merit, nor in cause and effect, nor in the Triple Gem.
Those who are unfilial toward their kin are called the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). As for the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*),
if one is immersed in the five desires from moment to moment, craving many kinsmen and retinues, increasing day by day and month by month without ever reaching satiety;

They pervert principles and oppress others, never judging with impartiality; they seize wealth through illegality and act against righteousness solely to pursue their own profit, showing no compassion for the solitary or the poor.
They are openly greedy for the property of others, acting with brazen insolence and violence in the marketplace, refusing to pay what is owed while openly committing robbery.
Disloyal and unfilial, they are neither wise nor foolish; they do not believe in cause and effect, nor do they believe in the Three Jewels—stupid, shameless, and devoid of integrity.
Manifesting as members of the animal class is called the dharma-realm of animals.
As for the realm of hell,
if one associates with evil teachers and friends, or by one's own nature commits evil and gives rise to an intensified mind, moment after moment they [succeed one another].
To further commit the ten grave evils—namely, killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, frivolous speech, double-tongued speech, harsh abuse, greed, anger, and wrong views;
to befriend those who have committed the five heinous crimes or violated the four grave prohibitions; to defile those who practice the precepts; to sell wine to cause intoxication and disorder;

to fail to reflect upon the kindness and virtue of rulers, parents, and teachers; to recklessly give rise to feverish afflictions; to suppress the worthy and capable; and to side with the unworthy—this is [the nature of such conduct].

They go so far as to destroy stupas and monasteries, burn and annihilate scriptures and images, slander and revile the Mahāyāna, sever the study of Prajñāpāramitā, deny the existence of all Buddhas, violate the precepts,
and accept offerings by misappropriating the property of the Three Jewels or stealing the goods of the Saṃgha. They commit every such evil without exception,
giving rise to the various views of permanence and annihilation held by non-Buddhists, subverting the true law of cause and effect across the three periods of time, and even practicing...
The twelve types of unwholesome modes of conduct (*akuśala-asaṃvara*) are: first, the butcher; second, the executioner;
third, the pig-breeder; fourth, the poultry-keeper; fifth, the fisherman; sixth, the hunter; seventh, the bird-catcher; eighth, the python-trapper;
ninth, the dragon-charmer; tenth, the jailer; eleventh, the thief; and twelfth, one who constantly serves the royal household as a hunter.
Those such as thieves, silkworm breeders, and others of this ilk who die and fall into the eight great hells, such as the Avīci Great Intense Heat Hell,
and traverse the path of blazing fire, are called the Dharma-realm of the hells.
The verse says:
In the three realms there is no separate dharma; All is created solely by the mind. Therefore, day and night, one should diligently observe the mind for oneself.
If the mind desires to give rise to various evils, One must extinguish them swiftly, as if putting out a fire.
When the mind desires to give rise to various virtues, protect them as if they were precious jewels.

Though the practice of evil may last but a brief moment, the suffering one undergoes in the future will be long-lasting. To perform good deeds directed toward Bodhi is to eternally realize the fruit of perpetual bliss;
this is the method for adorning the ten realms with their various forms and characteristics.
Regarding the ten types of colored adornments representing the radiance of the mind and the forms of the world: the Buddha-realm is made golden; the Bodhisattva-realm is made five-colored;
the two realms of Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas are made the color of blue space; the realm of devas is made a superior white;
humans are made white; asuras are made yellow; hungry ghosts are made blue; animals are made red; and the hells are [made black].
Those who appear black are only ten kinds of people, whose complexions remain as they usually are; all other lands appear as empty space.

One who contemplates this diagram shall perceive each individual’s vibrant spirit and come to know clearly the manifest beauty or ugliness of their retribution, arising from the causal conditions of their good and evil karma.
Huilin Daxu Yikong respectfully records this:
The End of the Diagram of the Ten Dharma Realms for Contemplating the Mind According to the Perfect and Sudden Teaching.
Presented to Prime Minister Wang Qinruo. Verses on the Diagram of the Ten Realms of the Mind.
Without form and without name, it is profound and beyond seeking; one forcibly uses names and forms to fathom the mysterious depths. Relying on this to understand, one instead turns away from it;

abandoning it here to seek elsewhere, one sinks further into delusion. On Vulture Peak, the instruction was earnestly and personally entrusted; at Dragon Gate, the kindness was such that he sought those who could truly know him.
Yet it is still heard that it hangs upon the high hall, where it mistakenly kills the passerby and causes them to misrecognize their own mind.
Record of the Sandalwood Image of the Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara (Along with) the Text of the Fourteen Vows:
From the time the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the fourth Tathāgata of the Bhadrakalpa, entered Mahāparinirvāṇa until now, one thousand nine hundred and forty-nine years have passed.

From the time Dharmaratna and Kāśyapa-mātanga crossed over to China and the Great Dharma gradually spread to the East, nine hundred and thirty-three years have passed. [Since the arrival of] Saṃghavarman...
It has been seven hundred and seventy-one years since the arrival [of Buddhism] in the region east of the Yangtze River during the Wu dynasty.

In the year of Jihai, the third year of the reign of the Great Song’s Renxiao Emperor, when the Emperor—possessing the qualities of reverence, clarity, and reflection—had personally ascended the throne and brought the world under his enlightened rule, he honored both kin and subjects, and from high to low, all were clad in the robes of Confucianism and Buddhism, jointly devoted to spiritual cultivation. In the fourth month of that year, at Siming...
The Śramaṇa Zunshe carved this sandalwood image and inscribed it with his own hand, stating:
"How fortunate is I, Zunshe! Having left the household life to study the Way, I have encountered the Dharma-gate of wondrous realization taught by the Tiantai Master Zhizhe.
The general outline of that Dharma-gate directly points to body and mind as the secret treasury."

The teaching of this school is the proclamation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Nirvāṇa* sūtras as the "cream of the cream" (*paramamṛdu*), and the practice cultivated is the gate of the perfect and sudden *Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
Every single word and principle encompasses both the provisional and the real, the partial and the perfect, the small and the great;
the Buddha-dharma of the three periods of time is contained therein. What noble guest has not received its benefit? Thus, for a long time, I have studied under him.

Tomorrow evening I shall return to Tiantai. Because I have compiled the *Ten Sections on the Ritual for Invoking Avalokiteśvara* by hand, it is precisely the method of samādhi from the fourth fascicle of the *Mohe Zhiguan*.
Whenever I personally practice this method, I dare not be negligent; if I were to assist others as well, I would certainly rely upon its power.
How admirable! The Great Sage benefits my own person with the benefit of non-action. I shall lead [others] forth.
The benefit of one's own person lies in benefiting others; indeed, among the essentials of the Way of Benefit, none is more magnificent than this:

to induce them by means of manifesting spiritual resonance, to inform them by means of ritual forms and images, to bring peace to the Imperial State through assistance, and to provide guidance by disseminating the True Teaching.
When these four elements are complete, one may attain the state of non-action (*wuwei*). Having initiated these fourteen vows, I pray that they may assist the State.

The exposition of the teachings is set at the beginning of the volume; next follows the ritual for invoking the sacred image. According to the *Sūtra on the Entrustment of the Golden Coffin*, one should strictly purify the site.
According to the *Eleven-Faced Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*, the body of the statue should be carved from flawless white sandalwood.

According to the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa Sūtra*, [the deity] has seven heads and six arms. According to the *Mahākaruṇā Sūtra* and the *Ratna-samādhi Sūtra*, [the hands] hold a precious seal, a peach of the immortals, and a lotus.
Having finished copying the Flower Garland Sūtra, the Dantakāṣṭha Sūtra, and the Kamaṇḍalu Sūtra, he knelt before the image to serve as its seat.

He placed a lotus flower upon his head to receive the holy feet of the Buddha. Using gold dust as ink, he inscribed the *Ratnaketuparivarta Sūtra*, the *Sarvadurgatipariśodhana Dhāraṇī*, and the three chapters of the *Ātānātika Dhāraṇī* within a fragrant banner, which he then inserted into the belly of the image.
As for the *Dhyāna on the Image* (Kuan-hsiang fa-men), this image already manifests its full realization.
The aggregates that bind are the Tathāgatagarbha; this is the realm of Avalokiteśvara. The Bodhisattva image represents one who is capable of contemplation.

The seven heads signify the Great One’s *sarvajñājñāna* (all-encompassing wisdom); the remaining six represent the *pāramitās*. These perfections, when cultivated to completion, take *sarvajñājñāna* as their guide, and thus all are termed "heads.
Furthermore, the "heads" possess many faculties, which are the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*). The "Great Head" is specifically the factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Collectively, among the remaining six, they occupy the center. The jewel seal and the jewel scripture specifically represent the realm and wisdom of self-cultivation.

The lotus and the peach represent the transcendence of cause and fruit to the upper [realm]. The willow branch and the bathing flask represent the transformation through concentration and wisdom in the lower [realm].

The flower has forty-one petals in total, representing the perfect true cause. The peach has only four fruits, representing the constant and blissful fruit. The willow branch’s swaying represents wisdom.
The water in the vase is clear and still, representing meditative concentration (*samādhi*); the two feet represent compassion (*karuṇā*). As the Sūtra says:
"With great kindness and great compassion, they sport within the five realms of existence"—this signifies the feet.

The lotus beneath the feet has forty-two petals in total, universally symbolizing that the ground of cause and the ground of fruition are both supported by unconditioned compassion. The jeweled clouds beneath the flower manifest the aspect of compassion; these clouds...
The canopy provides shade and rain; shade removes heat and extracts suffering, while rain provides moisture and bestows joy.

Therefore, its placement above the head of the image signifies the covering and nourishing of sentient beings. The fineness of every tooth and hair is fashioned as gateways to the Dharma (*dharmamukha*);

the solemnity of the crown and pendants all symbolize the myriad virtues. There is no need for further detailed record. Written by the Bhikṣu Baochan upon encountering the lamp while transcribing the Golden Letter Sutra.

The lay devotee Jiatiao (Ji Zhitiao) commissioned the carving of this image by Shen Jingyue. The features were refined by Zhang Jingxiu, and the grand purity of its virtue was cultivated by Yu Jingxin.
With the necessary materials for the image provided, its construction finally commenced within the Great Dharma Hall. He summoned some one hundred monks from the district;
as the sun set, they arrived and performed the recitation of the sutras and the Dharma, invoking Avalokiteśvara to bear witness to it.
Homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time! Homage to the Original Teacher, the Great Muni!
Homage to the Land of Peace and Bliss in the West, To Amitābha Buddha, Honored One of the Ten Powers!
Homage to Avalokiteśvara, The Lamp of the World in every age throughout incalculable past kalpas!
The wisdom-eye of all Buddhas is foremost in purity; Observing the triple world through the mark of non-duality, they see it as it truly is.
I take refuge and pay homage to them who have accomplished great vows to protect sentient beings.
Homage to the ocean of all Dharma-jewels, With its boundless and inexhaustible gates of liberation.
Homage to the Treasury of Dhāraṇī Merits! The seal of all Buddhas of the three periods and ten directions, It eliminates the three obstacles and removes all evils;
Endowed with the five eyes, one attains Bodhi, Vowing to practice through future kalpas until the end of time, Universally causing all sentient beings to obtain fearlessness.
Homage to Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, the Honored Ones; To Sarvajñācāraparipūrṇasāgara, Vajragarbha, and Vajrapāṇi;
To Mahāsthāmaprāpta and all other great beings, as well as the assembly of noble Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and sages— May you all look upon us with eyes of compassion.
I now take refuge in and praise the Triple Gem, desiring to plunge deeply into the ocean of great compassion.
Since I have encountered the Buddha Avalokiteśvara in the past and entered the gateway of that Tathāgata,
the Buddha has bestowed upon me a name identical to his own.
Through hearing, one is liberated from the bonds of the six sense objects;
Just as sound passes through a wall without obstruction, One thereby enters universally into lands as numerous as motes of dust, Universally manifesting autonomous bodies within each mote of dust.
Each body proclaims the phrases of *dhāraṇī*, Bestowing upon sentient beings the Dharma of fearlessness.
Therefore, throughout the Sahā world, I am universally known as the Bestower of Fearlessness.
In the past, I encountered this secret mantra within the sūtras; it is capable of eliminating the three obstructions and is called "The Subduing and Eliminating.
Its merits are said to be inconceivable, and thus I constantly uphold it, never daring to forget it.
I vow that throughout the ocean of future great kalpas, I shall universally use these words to rescue all from suffering;
seeking the power of the Great Being’s empowerment,
I have fashioned this sandalwood image of the mantra-holder with a Śaṅkara head and golden countenance, complete with the seven numbers of dignified marks.
The Mātṛkā-bāhu [statue], possessing hundreds of thousands of merits, has six successive hands holding various items:
a palm-leaf manuscript, a jeweled seal, a flower, fruit, a water-pitcher, and a tooth-stick.
Carved from flawless white sandalwood, each one was fashioned in accordance with the sūtras.
And I, prostrating myself on the ground, take refuge in the name of the auspicious and blissful one, Avalokiteśvara, relying upon his true concentration; may he surely hear my present great vow.
O Muni, the scriptures, the images, and the community of bhikṣus—may you remain in the world forever without perishing.
Protecting the land and its sentient beings, universally causing them to embrace the vow for bodhi;
may the Three Jewels, the divine mantras, the devas, nāgas, and others, through the power of their great compassion and great vows,
all together protect this sacred ritual of the Honored One, remaining forever indestructible like a vajra.
Thus have I fulfilled these fourteen vows, All for the sake of enlightenment and all sentient beings.
Homage to the one who rescues from calamity upon hearing his name! Homage to the compassionate father of the world!
Homage to the one who bestows upon me the power of fearlessness! Homage to the one who causes my wishes to be fulfilled!
Those who hear the name, see it, or contemplate it in body and mind— I now take refuge in all [Buddhas] so that my efforts may not be in vain;
I shall now set forth my successive vows. May the Honored One listen fully and individually to each:
(1) The vow to protect the land; (2–4) The vows to protect the Three Jewels; (5–7) The vows to protect sentient beings; (8) The vow to protect the Dharma in the future.
Ninth to Eleventh: The Original Vows for Bodhi; Twelfth to Fourteenth: The Vows for Protecting Incense and Images. The First Vow:
May the sacred body of the Myō-ō (Vidyārāja), who protects the Righteous Dharma of the Imperial Nation, remain in good health; may his divine mandate endure for a long time;
may he compassionately oversee the myriad nations and pity the four classes of living beings; and may the Empress, the consorts, and all those in the palace serve him with sincere hearts.

Providing the foundation for welfare, they long preserve honor and joy; as ministers and officials of the various bureaus across the five ranks, they protect the state and bring peace to the people, assisting and supporting for ten thousand generations.
Throughout the four seas, transformation spreads as the people become sincere and clear about righteousness. Auspicious winds and sweet rains nourish all things according to the seasons;

ears of grain form together and melons grow in succession, manifesting their virtue at the appointed time. Only then do they establish faith in the Triple Gem and plant goodness in the Three Fields, becoming sages of the nation.
The worthies of the court have examined phenomena to accord with principle, ensuring that the orthodox teaching is not misrepresented; their devotion has a clear direction.

They assist the Enlightened King in jointly propagating the Buddha-dharma and extensively establishing stupas and images, deeply honoring the Mahāyāna. The virtuous influence of these gentlemen causes the myriad subjects to submit with joy;

from the highest to the lowest, they honor the orthodox and sever the heterodox. The five blessings are bestowed upon the people, and the six perfections save all beings. Throughout the entire nation, there is pure joy, as serene as a clear mirror.
Regarding the Buddha-lands:
my second vow is that all images, relics, and stupas of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas,
and Pratyekabuddhas throughout the great trichiliocosm of the Sage’s True Dharma shall remain in this land forever, never to perish or decay.

All the stupas of King Aśoka, the statues of King Indrānuśāsaka, the two statues from the Wu region, the auspicious statue of Tao Kan, and others such as these—renowned stupas and images—may they remain forever in this world.

May benevolent kings and worthy believers protect them with sincere faith as treasures of the nation, so that they may bring forth blessings and prosperity and gloriously support the Way and its Virtue.
From time immemorial, wherever there have been superior stupas and images in mountains, marshes, or villages...
When the time for the disappearance [of the teachings] arrives, may those with faith who wish to construct [shrines] encounter favorable conditions and swiftly achieve success.
May stūpas and temples always adorn the realm, universally increasing the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha,
causing the realms of gods and humans to flourish while diminishing the evil paths.
The third vow is that the Dharma-treasury of the Three Vehicles within the teachings of the Muni’s Buddha-dharma shall be propagated throughout all lands without decline;
wherever it is disseminated— even down to a single verse or a single phrase— the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas,
shall diligently provide protection to eliminate obstacles and difficulties, constantly creating auspiciousness wherever there are scriptures, and causing all realms to be abundant and joyful.
Should there be calamities that invade the country and harm the people, may all Bodhisattvas immediately emerge from their realms to lecture and recite the sutras,
so as to eliminate disasters, repel enemies, and cause the ruler, the ministers, and all the people of the land who possess right faith to fully protect the Buddha-dharma;
may they widely transcribe the sutra scrolls so that the True Dharma may abide for a long time, serving as a boat for crossing the sea of suffering.
The fourth vow is: May all bhikṣus of Jambudvīpa—whether they observe the precepts fully or partially, or even down to those who have no precepts at all;

whether they are learned or have little learning, or even down to those who are unlearned—be universally peaceful and secure, meeting no national calamities, and be provided with the requisites of faithful offerings, gardens, and dwellings.
May those who possess the precepts and much learning quickly realize the stages of the Path; may those who lack the precepts and learning feel self-reproach and advance.
If a student-monk should break the precepts and feel no shame, I pray that the king, ministers, faithful patrons, and donors will not see his faults;
whether he acts in violation or in accordance with the rules, may they protect him with a heart of loving-kindness.

If he should violate the laws of the state and require legal punishment, may he not be disgraced in the marketplace, but rather be pardoned. I pray that the King will release him with compassion, especially during times of national celebration.

I pray that upon my enthronement, I may deliver sentient beings by leaving the household life to assist the auspicious fortune of the nation, ensuring that the Three Jewels shall never be interrupted.
My fifth vow is for all sentient beings who cling to existence and falsely claim that the Tathāgata has truly entered nirvana, causing the True Dharma to diminish;
for those whose attachment to worldly teachings causes their hearts to become distant and their mindfulness of the True Cause and Effect to grow thin, I vow to cause them to develop correct faith.
These faithless sentient beings constantly encounter virtuous friends who instruct them in right view and cause them to deeply revere the Mahāyāna.
They understand in accordance with reality that the Buddha does not pass into extinction, that he does not follow worldly appearances, and that there is neither birth nor death.

What is called "nirvāṇa" refers to the Tathāgata’s eternal tranquility, his abandonment of all fetters and delusions, and his pure fulfillment of merit and wisdom, after which there is nothing further to be done. This is its name.
For the sake of nirvāṇa, those sinful sentient beings perceive coming and going, which is not the work of the Tathāgata. The Triple Gem is eternally abiding, illuminating throughout the long night.
How is this known? The *Mahāmegha Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata does not enter parinirvāṇa; the True Dharma is without extinction;
and the inconceivable Dharma-Saṃgha of the Tathāgata is likewise so. Upon hearing these words, one should practice with right faith.
I vow that I shall always delight in seeing the Buddha’s body and the places where his bodies are born, and that I shall not fall into the evil realms.
My sixth vow is: for the sake of those sentient beings who are attached to emptiness, who deny cause and effect, and who practice only non-obstruction while neglecting the various precepts;

for those who have set their minds on the Lesser Vehicle and destroy [the teachings] without the slightest fear; and for those who themselves act thus and teach others, speaking [of such things as the truth].
The transmission of essential practices has spread like creeping vines, obscuring and destroying the eyes of sentient beings; together they are on the verge of falling into suffering.

I pray that those who have severed the roots of the lineage may encounter true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) who instruct them in right wisdom. May they apply themselves equally to both precepts and meditation, and be encouraged toward *nirvāṇa*, the Brahma-net, and the true reality (*tathatā*) of the Mahāyāna.

Just as one preserves the leather bag [of the Bodhisattva] or ties the grass [of the Śrāvaka], so too should they cultivate the fivefold Dharma-body; let both the Small and Great Vehicles be thus perfected through the six *pāramitās*.
"O Bhagavān, World-Honored One of the Two Feet, since you possess the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), having understood this,
I shall practice right conduct and swiftly fulfill the two adornments.
My seventh vow is that from this day forth until the end of the future, wherever I may be, I shall always be able to..."
He instructs all sentient beings to study the *bindus* (essential points), to completely abandon evil habits, and to practice virtuous deeds.

If they have violated their precepts, he teaches them to perform repentance; fearing the miserable realms, they find no peace until they are shown the various Mahāyāna *vaipulya* teachings so that they may adopt and practice them.
He shatters the three obstructions, even if they remain faithless and stubbornly cling to ignorance and delusion with arrogance.
"I vow never for even a moment to abandon the cultivation of various evils that increase my pride; may this follow me throughout all births.
I shall teach and transform them so that they gain right faith, just as Pure Treasury transformed King Adorned, causing them all to attain the Way of the Buddha."
The eighth vow is: May I, from this day forward, in the age of the Semblance Dharma (*śāsanadharma*) of the Muni, create images and make vows to protect the Buddha-dharma until the end of the future.

When the Buddhas, their images, and the Dharma are on the verge of declining, may I in those worlds create images of the Great Compassionate One and make great vows of compassion to protect the Triple Gem, causing it to abide for a long time and making the lamp of the Dharma blaze once more to illuminate and shatter [the darkness].
Throughout the long night, they have been transformed by the Buddha-sun into those who practice perfect equality.
For this reason, it would be better for them to sacrifice ten million bodies each day, with every limb reduced to fine dust, for the sake of protecting the Dharma;
they never grow weary or tired of this, let alone having any other thing to begrudge. They cherish only the Unsurpassed Way and never love their own bodies or lives, enduring all manner of suffering.
All these matters are for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
My ninth vow is: may this body of mine practice the Path in peace and security, free from all peripheral obstacles; may there be no difficulties regarding the True Dharma;

may the land be abundant and joyful; and may I always dwell in forests and wilds, delighting in solitude and stillness, wearing robes of rags and eating vegetables, being content with whatever is obtained according to my lot.
One should always fear offerings of faith as one would ward off a border enemy; always distance oneself from kinsmen as one would stay far from a great foe;

always preserve meditative concentration and wisdom as one would guard precious jewels; and always cast aside all evils as one would remove a chronic ailment. The Dharma robe and mendicant’s staff are armor and weapons for resisting Māra;
the meditation seat and incense jar are requisites for cultivating the Path. Beyond these, there is nothing else to crave—the habitual routines of worldly life.

May I not be drawn near to sensual desires, fame, or profit, which shall never follow me; may I regard praise and blame as empty echoes passing by the ear like the wind, remaining patient with both opposition and compliance so that my resolve for the path of practice remains complete.
My tenth vow is: may I always read the Mahāyāna, always expound the Mahāyāna, keep the matters of the Mahāyāna in mind, and contemplate the Great Vehicle.
Riding upon the meaning of the Great Vehicle, one practices the conduct of the Mahāyāna with a continuous stream of mind that never forgets the Great Vehicle.

One constantly recollects the vast ocean of Samantabhadra’s conduct, constantly contemplates the ocean of Samantabhadra’s impartial wisdom, constantly remembers Avalokiteśvara’s arising of the ocean of great compassion, and constantly remembers Maitreya’s practice of the ocean of great loving-kindness.
Whatever evil deeds are committed shall not succeed, while all cultivated roots of goodness shall be fully realized.

Through the integration of practice and vows, one is sustained by a body and mind at peace; afflictions gradually thin out, and through clear observation and tranquil stillness, one skillfully discerns the open and the obstructed.
Reaching the path of security, one clings not to the good and follows not after evil.
With these ten dharmas forming the vehicle, one’s stride is level and upright, swiftly reaching the site of enlightenment where wisdom and vows are fulfilled.

The eleventh vow is: May this body of mine constantly repent of all karmic actions, so that at the end of life, I shall not, due to evil causes and conditions, return to this world or to the eight difficult states (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*).

Should there be evil karma that ought to cause me to fall into the evil realms, may the Three Jewels protect and mind me, and by the power of my vow, extend [the consequences] until the stage of non-arising forbearance (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); rather than [suffering for] a single karma, may it be [exhausted] through countless [lifetimes].
I dare not regard this as labor, for I shall repay you twofold. Now, there are two reasons why I pray that my life may end swiftly so that I may be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss:

First, in this age of the semblance Dharma, worldly customs are diluted and pure precepts are difficult to maintain; it is hard to keep even the rules regarding water and food, let alone other precepts.

I fear that by violating the prohibitions, I would fall into suffering for a long time, thereby obstructing my cultivation of the path and its practices. Second, I desire to quickly achieve accomplishment in order to deliver sentient beings.

If the causes and conditions for reaching that land, seeing the Buddha, awakening to the Way, and accomplishing the task should arise, may these two conditions enable me to quickly attain rebirth there and fulfill my vow for Bodhi.
As for the twelfth vow: regarding the great holy incense image I have fashioned, with its ordinary human body, arms, and feet, may it hold a pair of sandals.

The jar-branch crown bearing blossoms and fruits, with its silk streamers and pendants all complete, represents all *dharmamukhas*: whether the nature of cultivation or the wisdom of the objective realm;

the cause and fruit of one's own practice, or the samādhi and prajñā for transforming others; the six *pāramitās*, the four immeasurables, and even down to the teeth and hair—all are manifested as *dharmamukhas*.
If this slightly accords with the Sage’s heart, I pray that you add the power of your compassion so that this wondrous image may become like the Great Being himself.

The emanated bodies that flow forth to transform beings throughout the infinite heavens and the human realm always manifest their influence, universally enabling those with karmic affinity to extinguish the seven calamities and the three poisons through this very means.
The thirty-three bodies and the nineteen modes of preaching the Dharma are all felt through this;
the Three Jewels and the Four Noble Truths are manifested thereby. Its light shines upon all phenomena, acting as the seed, the maturation, and the cause for liberation, causing [beings] to...
The five realms are empty and void, and the source of rebirth is exhausted;
yet if one harbors an evil mind to destroy my holy image, they thereby destroy the body of Avalokiteśvara, destroy the body of future Buddhas, and destroy all the True Dharma.

Such a person truly severs the seeds of the Triple Gem, is a great enemy to sentient beings, robs them of all happiness and bestows all suffering, and extinguishes the light in the great darkness of night.

To extinguish the lamps and torches in the deep and vast ocean, to destroy others' ships and rafts, or likewise to amputate a person's feet, gouge out their eyes, and cast them into ditches and drains—there is no evil in the world that exceeds such sin.
Even if one were to kill one's parents a hundred thousand times over, the one who kills their parents receives the retribution themselves;
yet if one defiles this image, the calamity and suffering will extend to all. As the Sūtra says: "It shall cause..."
Those who hear the name of this Great Compassionate One are protected by him as a royal minister protects a sovereign, and as the devas serve Śakra.

Should anyone oppose this mantra and give rise to unwholesome thoughts, they will manifest leprosy in this life, with pus and blood flowing from their bodies, and shall subsequently fall into hell to suffer for a long night.
If people hear of this and commit the grave sin of slander, they should be careful not to harbor even a single thought of lack of faith, much less go so far as to revile it.

[The thirteenth vow: "I have already caused the *Baoxi yin jing* (Treasure Casket Seal Sutra), the *Xiaofu duhai po eyezhangju san tuoluoni* (Dhāraṇīs of the Six-Syllable Phrase for Subduing Poisonous Harm and Destroying Obstacles of Evil Karma),
and the three dhāraṇīs to naturally and constantly emanate from within the precious incense-banner."
May the light shine through all Buddha-fields in the ten directions; may the World-Honored Buddhas, as described in the sutras,
always follow this image wherever it may be located throughout all time, using their powers of supernatural penetration (*abhijñā*) and the power of their vows to empower,
protect, and keep in mind the Vajra-treasury of all Tathāgatas, Śakra, and the devas by day.
Descending at the three periods of the night, they offer worship to all the ṛṣis and devas; day and night, at the three periods, they sing hymns and offer praises.
If there are sentient beings who plant roots of virtue before this image, they will certainly attain non-retrogression from the Bodhi of the Buddha.
Even those who would otherwise fall into hell, if they perform a single prostration or a single circumambulation before this image, shall surely obtain [liberation].
Those who are thus exempt from the heavy sufferings of hell cannot be oppressed by any poison or harm.

Should anyone wish to destroy them, they would thereby be violating and destroying the hearts of all Buddhas, the Buddha-uṣṇīṣas, the Buddha-eyes, the bodies of all Buddhas, the collection of all Buddha-relics, and the treasury of the True Dharma of all Buddhas;
having destroyed all these, they would likewise be in opposition to all devas, ṛṣis, and nāgas. Twenty.

May all the spirits and deities of the eight classes wish that when worldly people hear this teaching of the Buddha, they will believe it deeply; that those who commit acts of destruction shall incur immeasurable sin;
and that they shall swiftly cease their evil intentions, give rise to right faith, and protect and make offerings [to the Triple Gem] as if it were their own life, no different from themselves.

The fourteenth vow is as follows: I entreat the Northern Śrīmaṇḍala-mahārāja, Mahāśrīdevī, and all the retinues of the great yakṣas to protect my image so that it may remain forever in the world, extensively performing acts of benefit.
Should anyone, even for a brief moment, pay homage and offer worship with a sincere heart, [may they... all...
The celestial hosts shall immediately bestow upon that person great auspiciousness, precious treasures, official rank, honor, retinue, longevity,
and the fulfillment of all wishes. Should wicked people, wild beasts, evil spirits, malevolent dragons, or even sparrows, mice, mosquitoes, and gadflies seek to invade or destroy them,
the hosts of yakṣas will swiftly provide protection like a flash of lightning, taking care not to let even a hair’s tip of harm come to them.
I grant permission to well protect all the mental thoughts of sentient beings, so that they do not give rise to even a moment’s lack of faith toward my image;
should anyone give rise to such lack of faith, they shall receive an extremely evil retribution. For this reason, you should always protect them with a heart of loving-kindness.
To protect them with a heart of loving-kindness is itself to well protect all sentient beings, and it is also to well protect all Buddhas.
It is likewise with the mind, all true dharmas, all bodhi, and all roots of goodness.

When the conditions for this image of mine to transform the world have ended, may Śvetambara take it to the celestial realm to protect and make offerings to the image of Maitreya’s Dharma, and then return here once more; even when the Buddhas come, it shall be the same.
Homage to the Buddha! Homage to the Dharma! Homage to the Saṅgha! Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara of Great Compassion!

I have fully brought forth these fourteen kinds of vows; may the Three Jewels and their great compassion bear witness to me, causing each and every vow to be fully accomplished, so that the Three Jewels may abide forever and the gift of Dharma remain inexhaustible. I vow...
In the future, in every world of the Buddhas and their Dharma, for the sake of protecting the Dharma, I shall create images of fearlessness and make pure vows no different from those made now.
Each image created shall remain undestroyed through successive lifetimes, filling the ten directions until there is not a single gap of space left empty;
I too shall never rest until the appearance of every Buddha has ceased, at which point I shall finally cease. If it were the Buddha...
Sentient beings never come to an end, and my creation of this image and the making of this vow shall likewise never end.
For this reason, I shall again speak in verse to praise the Greatly Compassionate King of Physicians who saves the world, so that all sentient beings may always give rise to right faith.
The verse says:
O Greatly Compassionate One of Great Renown, Auspicious and Bringer of Peace and Bliss, I have fashioned this supreme image, And I have made this supreme vow:
To protect the Dharma of the Muni So that it may long abide in the world.
The Muni, through long cultivation, attained An immeasurable lifespan; For the sake of all sinful sentient beings, [May he remain for as long as space endures.]
It is conventionally said that there is parinirvāṇa, As well as the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma, Which gradually diminish;
yet beings, blinded by ignorance, Truly believe such things exist.
Just as the Sun Deity circles Mount Sumeru day and night, The foolish do not understand this, And claim that the sun rises and sets.
Light and darkness give rise to sorrow and joy; Labor has its periods of activity and rest.
But for that King of Sunlight, such things truly do not exist. The Three Jewels are the lamps that illuminate the world; They abide eternally, neither brightening nor extinguishing.
Yet, to accord with deluded sentient beings, They appear as if coming and going. I wish to shatter these inversions.
Having given rise to right faith, one should understand all things: Buddha, Dharma, Saṃgha—ever-abiding.
Namo Avalokiteśvara, The one who can bestow fearlessness, Who always dwells in the Sahā world to save these suffering sentient beings.
I now praise you again, Increasing my vow for Bodhi.
With the most purified divine ear, listen to my verses:
Your wondrous marks are golden light, and the seven heads shine with brilliance, Like the seven golden mountains, towering high above the heavens.
Therefore, I pay homage to you, whose body surpasses the world and is peerless, And whose brow-hair is like the full moon of the seventh month.
Shining upon a mass of pure gold, Their intermingling radiance is brilliantly clear, Illuminating the lands of the ten directions;
Therefore, I pay homage with my head bowed. With light that removes heat and brings cooling clarity, Long eyes are shaded by well-grown brows, Like fragrant blue lotuses in a verdant pool.
Perfumed by the power of benevolence and compassion, My gaze upon you can never be satiated.
Therefore, I pay homage to him who regards all sentient beings with equality; To him whose chest is level and whose radiance blazes forth like the lion, king of beasts;
Whose pearl necklaces interlace in shimmering light, like stars scattered across the azure void.
Therefore, I pay homage to him whose aspect of loving-kindness is vast and wide; To his arms, adorned with the merit of a hundred blessings.
Golden light swirls, perfectly full and exceedingly soft, like the trunk of a king of elephants; therefore, I bow my head in homage.
You have uprooted the suffering of the three realms of existence; the soles of your feet are as level as a casket, adorned with the pure and beautiful thousand-spoked wheels.
With hundreds of thousands of millions of rays of light, you are magnificently adorned and shine everywhere.

Therefore, I pay homage: Constantly wandering through the realms of the five destinies, With such boundless forms, each permeated by kindness and compassion, The ocean of merit is full to overflowing, And its radiant flames shine infinitely.
Therefore, I pay homage: The ocean of accumulated blessings is immeasurable, And the fragrance of the body is pure and sublime.
Like a cluster of lotuses, those sentient beings who are perfumed by them develop supple bodies and virtuous minds;
therefore, I pay homage with my head bowed. Excellent is Avalokiteśvara, whose light of wisdom destroys all darkness;
excellent is the King of Supernatural Powers, whose fragrance of virtue perfumes all.
Therefore, I pay homage with my head to the Honored One who is fully endowed with the two adornments;
To all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, each seated upon a lion throne, With tongues shaped like lotus petals and lips the color of the *bimba* fruit,
I praise the Great Compassionate One, that ocean of profound and vast merit, Which could not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.
The sovereign activity of the Universal Gate manifests throughout the worlds of the ten directions;
each and every form is boundless, saving all from the sufferings of existence, from urgent calamities, and from all fears. Who would not receive your compassionate protection?
Therefore, I pay homage with my head to the Compassionate Father of the World; may I establish this supreme image.
May my body of supernormal powers remain eternally, unchanging and indestructible;
Like the most supreme vajra, may all who gaze upon it with reverence find auspiciousness.
May they shatter the suffering of the three obstructions and all attain transcendental bliss. I entreat the Deva of Great Learning to protect this wondrous incense image.
May you exert the power of great compassion to cause those gods to rejoice.
O Lord of Auspicious Merit, who accomplishes all tasks, may you conceal your celestial form day and night.
Together with the Yakṣa Mahātejas, who provides steadfast protection, may you move through the world without fear for the sake of all sentient beings.
May all virtuous merits be steadfastly protected;
may the supreme portion always be offered to the northern celestial retinues and Śrīdevī, so that all may rejoice.
May the vow for the fulfillment of enlightenment be realized. If there be a king among men, his ministers, and all his officials—
When pure men and women behold my sublime form for even a moment, they shall all obtain the fulfillment of every wish—be it merit, wisdom, or long life.
It may be that the great earth is overturned, that the sun and moon cease to move, or that empty space suddenly takes on form and obstructs the passage of people; yet such things could never happen.
The Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara, There is no wish of man that he does not fulfill. Namo Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha;
Namo to the Honored One of Great Compassion. I prostrate with my whole being to you all. May you graciously accept me with compassion.
I have briefly praised this assembly of fearlessness and supernormal powers.
The First Account of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva’s Responsive Manifestations in Eliminating the Seven Calamities:
The Scripture on the Calamity of Fire states, "If there are those who hold the name of this Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, even if they enter a great fire, the fire shall not burn them.
The Record of Verified Responses states that a monk named Fǎlì was transporting hemp in the open wilderness of Shànggǔ when—
Once, while encountering a fire, he was initially so exhausted that he fell asleep for a moment; when he woke up, the flames had already reached him.

He raised his voice and invoked Avalokiteśvara, and as soon as he uttered the name, the fire was extinguished. There are many such instances; this is merely one example shown in brief. The *Tiantai Shu* states:
"Whether it be the fire of karmic retribution, the fire of evil karma, or the fire of afflictions that burns within the three realms, by invoking Avalokiteśvara, all are saved."
Liberation. The second, the *Sutra on the Peril of Water*, states: "If one is being swept away by a great flood, by invoking his name, one will immediately find shallow ground.
The *Records of Verified Responses* relates: "In the past, Liu Cheng accompanied Fei Yan to Guangzhou; upon reaching Guantang, they encountered a storm. Liu Cheng’s mother..."
Furthermore, as the voices of two nuns chanted the name of Avalokiteśvara without ceasing, he suddenly saw two people supporting the boat and they were able to reach the shore;
Fatai’s wife was on a separate boat, and while other boats all sank and failed to cross, this was one of many such instances.
Tiantai said: "The water of karmic retribution, the water of evil karma, and the water of afflictions sweep away all beings; yet by invoking his name, all are saved."
They attain liberation.

The *Third Sūtra on the Peril of Rākṣasīs* states: "If there are people who, seeking treasures such as gold and silver, enter the great ocean and are driven by black winds into the land of rākṣasa demons;
if even one person among them utters the name of Avalokiteśvara, then all these people [shall be saved]."
The *Account of Miraculous Responses to Liberation* states that one hundred foreigners sailing by sea toward Funan encountered a storm and were driven adrift into a land of ghosts.
Those ghosts intended to take all the people to eat them; the crew was terrified and everyone invoked the name of Avalokiteśvara.
Among them was a śramaṇa of the Hīnayāna who did not believe in Avalokiteśvara and refused to call upon his name, whereupon the ghosts finally seized him.
This śramaṇa alone wished to devour him; out of fear of the śramaṇa, [the demon] hastily called out [the name], and thus he was also able to escape. Tiantai said:
"The retribution-rākṣasa, the karma-rākṣasa, and the affliction-rākṣasa all devour the practitioner’s body of merit;
if one calls upon the name, they are all liberated."

The fourth, the *Sūtra on the Peril of Weapons*, states: "When one is about to be harmed, if they invoke the name of Avalokiteśvara, the weapons held by the assailants will immediately break into pieces and they shall attain liberation.
The *Record of Verified Miracles* relates: During the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, Gao Jian committed a crime and was facing execution.

With single-minded devotion, he took refuge in the Buddha; his shackles and chains vanished from sight, the sword struck against him broke, and when he was to be strangled with a rope, it snapped into fragments.
Having cut off [the debt], he then sold his wife and children and sold himself to raise funds for the construction of a five-story stupa as a repayment for the compassionate aid he had received.
Tiantai said: "Karmic retribution, evil deeds, afflictions, and the three poisons are all termed 'swords and arrows'; by invoking Avalokiteśvara, one attains liberation from them all."

The *Fifth Scripture on the Perils of Ghosts* states: "If yakṣas and rākṣasas fill a great trichiliocosm and come intending to harass people, upon hearing them invoke the name of Avalokiteśvara, these evil ghosts will not even be able to look at them with malevolent eyes, let alone inflict further harm.
The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* records that the śramaṇa Sengrong once exhorted a family to receive the bodhisattva precepts.

He had abandoned the sacrificial rites and diverted the divine objects for use within the Three Jewels. Later, while Sengrong was staying overnight at Daoxing Temple, he sat down to practice meditation.
Suddenly, he saw a ghost leading countless ghost-soldiers, all clad in armor and equipped with swords and spears.
The ghost, appearing in a barbarian form, sat facing Rong and rebuked him, saying: "Why do you claim that ghosts and spirits have no spiritual power or sanctity? It was then...

In entering the bathhouse, one should briefly observe ten matters:
First, upon reaching the exterior door, one should first compose one’s demeanor and lift the curtain with light hands so that no wind is created.
Second, when avoiding senior monks (*zhūsù*) or elder monks (*shàngzuò*), one should know the proper places for putting on and taking off one's garments so as not to lose propriety.
When hanging three clean robes (*śuddhaka-cīvara*), they should be placed on a high rack; when touching them, they should be placed in a low location.

When drying the robes, one must not place them over the fire in the stove so that ash and flames fly upward. One must not shake or flap them to make a noise. When drying clean robes, they should be placed on a high spot;
when touching them, they should be placed on a low edge. Furthermore, one must yield to the *upādhyāya* (senior monk) and must not cover him with wet robes.
Do not obstruct others.
Fourth, one must not engage in idle chatter or laughter while at the bathing place; one must not call out loudly or cough and spit excessively.

When sitting, one should be mindful of those above and below, covering the body with a towel. Furthermore, one must not touch the hanging clothes or use the partition boards as a screen. Do not allow [the water] to...

When ashes or soap are scattered and disarrayed, one should use a ladle to scoop up the ashes and place them between the thighs or upon a stool, ensuring that the ashes or soap do not drip into the wash basin.
Fifth, one must not scrub or wash against one another; instead, one should use a cloth held by both ends to rub the back, or use a wooden scrubber.
When scrubbing the body, do not rub against either side [of the vessel]. One must not let water from the washing cloth or other items drip into the trough while sitting next to others;
furthermore, one must not wash clothes within the hall.
Sixth, when washing the feet and lower limbs, one should hold a ladle with one hand and scrub with the other, pouring the hot water and ash from a distance.
Do not allow [the body] to be defiled by contact; once washed, one should rinse it two or three times, ensuring the hands are clean before taking turns holding the ladle.
When the sevenfold bathing is nearly finished, one must not stand up to pour water over the body; when the pouring of water is complete, one should first cover oneself with a clean towel.
One should turn the body over and back so as not to leave it exposed.
When exiting or entering, one should cover the body closely; one must not cover the lower parts with thin or sparse clothing, nor should one open or close doors or curtains so as to make a sound.
Ninth: When entering or exiting, do not let your shoes drag on the ground or make noise. Once you have put on your own footwear, you should return the communal shoes to their original place;
furthermore, you must cover your wet clothes so that they do not leave water droplets before the bed.
When putting on robes, one should first use another garment to cover the upper body; then, turning one's back, put on the inner shirt and skirt.
Once this is done, wash the hands and then put on the outer robe. If one loses a robe or sandals, one should search for them slowly and calmly, without raising one's voice.
If someone else has mistakenly taken them, one should request them back with kind words. When leaving the door, one should draw the curtain lightly so as not to make a sound.
The wind makes a sound.

Looking up to the precedent of the aforementioned details, one should act accordingly and must not allow any negligence; furthermore, it should be known that śrāmaṇeras and novice practitioners (tongxing) are not permitted to join the monks for communal bathing.
I have compiled and presented here the method for using the toilet.
Now, regarding the matter of bodily defilement and impurity, it appears in the golden words of the Great Sage and is recorded in the jade tablets of the various scriptures.

Yet those of later generations, with their coarse conduct, are unwilling to follow them, thereby inviting transgressions for themselves and bequeathing suffering from which they cannot easily escape. Thus, I now rely upon... [the following].
The Fifteen Articles on the Methods for Practice, compiled from the *Nanshan* and the *Three Thousand Codes of Deportment*, are hereby presented; please examine and carry them out in detail. 1.
When intending to enter or leave [the hall], one must prepare oneself early; one must not fail in decorum at the last moment. When desiring to relieve oneself, one should go immediately.
While walking, one must not pay respects to the *upādhyāya* (senior monk) on the path, nor should one receive the prostrations of others; one should keep the head slightly bowed and look ahead.
First, one must proceed upon the ground.
Second, one must know that when holding the water jar with bowed hands, the arms must not hang down.
Third, upon reaching the side of the latrine, one should know to yield to any venerable seniors who may be there.
Fourth, when approaching the latrine, one must first snap one's fingers three times or make a coughing sound; only if no one is there may one enter.
If someone is already inside, one must snap one's fingers and not crowd them.
Fifth, if many people are staying nearby and there is someone outside the latrine, one must leave the latrine immediately even if one has not finished, regardless of how urgent the need may be.
Having ascended six times and established oneself correctly, one should snap the fingers and then squat. When squatting correctly, one must not place one foot forward and the other foot behind;

nor should the body lean against anything. If it is night or in darkness, one should use a toilet scraper to draw lines back and forth within the hole to ascertain its length and width, as well as whether it is level or not.
Seventh: Adjusting the robe gradually according to the height of the pit, one must not lift it too high so as to expose the body;
the robe must be tucked in and not allowed to hang down into the pit. One must not swallow loudly or call out until the face turns red; one should gaze straight ahead and not look around or listen.
One must not lower the head to look into the pit, nor look at the private parts, nor touch the private parts with the hand.
8. One must not spit or discharge mucus on the walls, the four sides of the latrine, the wooden boards, or into the gutters and drains.
9. One must not use tally-sticks to scratch characters on the walls; when finished using a tally-stick, it must be placed back into its hole in the board and not left anywhere else.
After washing it ten times, one should use the water from the vessel conveniently for six or seven more washes.
If a bhikṣu does not wash it clean, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense; he shall not sit upon the monastic seating or pay homage to the Triple Gem, and even if he pays homage, there will be no merit.
Eleventh: When using water, one must not splash it about to make things wet, nor should one waste it excessively; furthermore, one must not allow the front hand to touch the back hand while using it.
Twelfth: When putting on or taking off footwear, one must not place clean shoes where they are normally stepped upon, nor should one touch the footwear [in such a manner].
One should wash [the hands] until they are clean.
Thirteenth: one should wash the hands until they are clean using yellow earth three or four times; one may also use soap powder, fine ash, or soap beans.
Furthermore, one must not leave ashes or dirt scattered in disarray; the area must be swept and tidied.
Fourteenth: One must always keep ready the toilet implements—such as wooden sticks, ash, soil, water, and soap—and ensure they are not lacking.
If one observes that any are missing or insufficient, one should inform the person in charge on duty; it is best if one takes them up with one's own hands.
Fifteenth: Seeing that the interior and exterior of the latrine are in disarray, one must constantly wash and sweep it to make it clean;

if the hand-towel is soiled with impurities, it must be washed until it is clean. Furthermore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If, after defecating or urinating, one uses a monastic seat, mat, or bedding without having washed [with water], one incurs an offense.
Moreover, the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states: "One must not enter the place for defecation or urination without having washed."
One does not commit an offense when prostrating in a place devoid of water, when one is being reviled by non-human beings or reviled by water deities, or when taking medicine and the like.

Furthermore, the *Sānqiānwēiyí jīng* (Sūtra on the Three Thousand Dignified Manners) states: "If one prostrates to the Buddha without having washed and purified oneself, even though one performs the prostration, there is no merit.
Moreover, the *Zápìyù jīng* (Sūtra of Various Parables) relates that there was once a bhikṣu who came without snapping his fingers and then urinated or defecated, splashing [the water].
Because he had defiled the face of a ghost, the demon became greatly enraged and desired to kill the śramaṇa who maintained the precepts;
the demon pursued him, watching for a weakness, but could find no opportunity. Knowing this matter, one must make a sound by clearing one's throat when entering the latrine.
